utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I have a few matters which I will leave until after we have concluded the testimony of this witness. I do understand that there was an issue to be raised by the Defence as well in relation to D631, but could we also leave that until after we have concluded the testimony of the present witness. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In the interim, if I could just do two things: One being a very short response to His Honour Judge Moloto's question of yesterday and that being, Your Honour, that the Prosecution's position with regard to your question is that the evidence in this case shows only a very small number of weapons in the Mahala area, and our position is that in any case there weren't weapons or forces of the number that would have justified the attack on the suburb. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the other small matter, Your Honour, being the pages that we saw in court yesterday of the witness's diary, 65 ter number 31847 which I wish to tender into evidence, have now been uploaded as 31847A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Registrar, could you assign a number to it or have you reserved a number for it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7070 was reserved, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Good morning, Mr. Karac. Before we continue, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Lukic will now continue his re-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Karac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we have P7015 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before it appears, I'm just going to tell you that it's the bulletin of the Serb Sanski Most, the Serb Democratic Party of Sanski Most. Yesterday this document was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need pages 38 in English and 25 in B/C/S. The penultimate paragraph in the English version and the third paragraph from the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that only part of your brigade took part in the disarming?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to remind you of something so let us take a look at a document here that the Prosecution tendered, P2411. So this is an order and it says here: Combat task disarmament operation in Sanski Most. It was signed by the commander of the Territorial Defence staff, Colonel Anicic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us take a look at page 2 in this document in B/C/S, and in English we're still on the first page. [In English] No, in English we stay on the same page, on the first page; and in B/C/S we need the second page. [Interpretation] So we need paragraph 3 that says that: "The 6th Brigade, in co-ordinated action with the Territorial Defence staff units, is undertaking combat operations in Sanski Most municipality area in order to disarm enemy forces by placing its main forces in the Skucani Vakuf-Kamengradska Dolina axis with emphasis on the general sector of Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here that units of the Territorial Defence are taking part. Did you know that, that units of the Territorial Defence took part in disarmament at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time who Colonel Anicic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us take a look at briefly at P3916.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The command of the 5th Corps on the 11th of May, 1992. And do focus on the last paragraph of this document where it says that your brigade took part in liberating the town of Bosanska Krupa. It is the 11th of May, 1992, as you can see in the document here and the document of the command of the 5th Corps. At the time, the 5th Corps, was it the JNA or the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Corps was a corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on it grew into which corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the document is from the period before the existence of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us take a look at P3294. This is Nedeljko Rasula's diary. We need page 19 in the English version of this document and the 16th page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which body Nedeljko Rasula headed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula was president of the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his role in the Crisis Staff, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think that as president he was supposed to be president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what we have before us here is the 14th of April, 1992, again a document from the period before the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, but never mind. I'm going to read it out to you in English what the Prosecutor put to you yesterday, and in this way you could get the right idea. 30722 is the transcript page. This is what my colleague said to you, line 14 onwards: [In English] "Here is a detailed plan for the Serb take-over of Sanski Most involving forces of your brigade. So you must have been a very bad intelligence officer if you didn't know anything about this plan for action." [Interpretation] Yesterday you told us that you as the intelligence organ followed the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document and the Prosecution's assertion that you were not a good intelligence officer if you didn't know about this plan of the Crisis Staff, this is what I'd like to ask you: Was it your duty to follow the work of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my duty was not to follow the work of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of Sanski Most, could they issue orders of the JNA or later on the units of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Crisis Staff never commanded the JNA and we had terrible problems there, also later on the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they try to command the units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out their orders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could we make that very concrete. Could you tell us about one or two orders you received which you then refused to carry out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that once the brigade commander told us that he received information that an attack was being prepared on the brigade command. That is what Colonel Basara said to us. And I know that one evening he gave us Zoljas and hand-grenades so that we could defend ourselves if we were to be attacked. So nobody exerted any pressure against me, but probably somebody was pressuring Colonel Basara to carry out certain tasks that he had probably refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all probabilities, nothing more than that. You don't know apparently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is about probabilities. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. No, I have one other question. Were you always opposed against interference in the command structures of the armed forces? Did you not accept anyone who was not in a formal position to give instructions or orders? Is that the situation that existed at the time, that the army would only act in accordance with the full hierarchical lines within the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we saw - I don't know whether you remember, otherwise we could call it up on the screen - we saw that the SDS Board, which is a party organ, said exactly what had to be done by units of the army. Is in your view that strictly in accordance with hierarchical lines within the army organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is interference in military hierarchy because we at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless we saw yesterday that such instructions were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw from the plan of the Territorial Defence staff. I never received an order like that from the Territorial Defence staff. I'm not denying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We looked yesterday at the SDS Municipal Board instructing which units should - as far as I remember - be there to secure the situation when the take-over took place. I'm referring to that example. You remember or don't you? Otherwise I have a look at it but I might need the assistance of the parties for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it's the same document. It's just page in English 22 and in B/C/S 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we have a look at it. I think it may be the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page in English --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I think if I recall correctly, I've just looked at my questions from yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You might be looking for page 21 in English, point number 2 and page 17 in B/C/S, if we're looking for the reference to the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the task given to provide security around -- yes, it was 2(a). There we see that the SDS Municipal Board gives instructions that a platoon of reservists in the 6th Krajina Brigade shall secure and control the bridge, square, park, municipal building, and post office. A minute ago you said that strictly obeying to the hierarchical army lines was what happened at the time, whereas this seems to me quite far away from that, where a party organ gives instructions to army units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I did say that they interfered with command over our units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check. One second, please. I asked you whether you did not accept any outside interference, whether that was the situation that existed at the time, that the army would only act in accordance with the full hierarchical lines within the army. You said: "That's the way it was at the time." And only after that you explained that it may have been different at the time. Now what --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, line 5 -- page 5, line 21, I asked: "Did they try to command the units?" And the witness in the next line answered: "Yes, they did."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you were asking about the Crisis Staff alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking a far broader question, and you may be aware that the example I am using now has got nothing to do with the Crisis Staff but it was the SDS Municipal Board. And therefore I asked -- let me try to summarise. You were asked whether the Crisis Staff tried to intervene. You gave an answer to that question that they did try. I asked you for one or two examples. You came up with an example, where as a matter of fact you talked about probabilities rather than about facts. Then I broadened the issue whether you accepted any outside interference at all in the hierarchical structure. Your answer was: We did not. That was the situation at the time. And then after that now I showed you the SDS Municipal Board giving instructions to the army. And it appears to me that you now agree that at that time one was not adhering strictly to army structures but that outside interference did happen. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such cases and as you can see in the document issued by the SDS, things like that did happen. However, the Territorial Defence staff was in control of those parts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking any further questions. Mr. Lukic, I also summarised the sequence of questions and answers for -- in order to make clear to you what was asked and what answers were given by the witness, which may also demonstrate that you inaccurately intervened. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, I did accurately intervene. We have to go several pages back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it was Crisis Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are not in a debating club.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in a court of law where the rulings are given by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back in the same document to page 38 in English and 25 in B/C/S. Actually now we have to go -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While you're finding your way, could I -- I think I said, and I'm looking at the transcript, that I -- page 10, line 5, that I said that "where the rulings are given by the Chamber." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I need date 14th of April, 1992, and it's -- next page, please. In B/C/S at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 14th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in English page 19 if I do not -- if I'm not mistaken, yes. 19 in English. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But this is 20th of April. We need 14th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14th of April I find in English on page 19 out of 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the sake of Mr. Karac, I think you probably want to direct him to page 16 in the document in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is -- this is the right page I have on the screen. We need the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- under number 4 and then it says 14th of April, 1992. It says that it was a course of action in taking over power in establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. And then -- yes, under number 4 already on the 14th of April it says -- we don't have I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have two entries starting with the 14th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the one starts at the bottom of page 19 in English and the other one is a few pages before that. Do we need this one because --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I need this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I don't have under number 4 in English where we need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the next page. That's page 20 where number 4, the Crisis Staff, is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on page 20. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But there is one part missing in English translation, I just noticed that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I will read it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Let's first try to establish exactly what is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's translated, sorry. It's underlined part when it says: "The Crisis Staff consisting of the following members" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- "shall be in charge of all actions ..." So after the 14th it's not actually the Municipal Assembly but Crisis Staff. And that's why I asked this gentleman whether the Crisis Staff interfered in commanding [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's apart from what I asked him later, whether there was any interference at all, irrespective from whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this same document on the following page -- [In English] So we'll need the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 2 it says: "The platoon of reservists from the 6th Krajina Brigade will secure, control the bridge, the park, the municipality building, the post office building ..." When it comes to guarding of the vital facilities in town, did that duty continue even after the take-over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever units and the command were deployed, yes, for the safety of those units. If units were not deployed, obviously there could be no guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When it comes to vital facilities, did you guard them also when you were in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the last bit of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also guard the vital facilities immediately upon deployment in the territory of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Sanski Most we were deployed and the deployment sectors were where we were and where we guarded facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you about Mahala. Do you know if Muslim fighters opened fire on Serbian troops from Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please repeat the question. I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Muslim soldiers open fire on Serbian soldiers who were on the scouring mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Muslim soldiers outside of Mahala arrive in Mahala on that day to fight or did they perhaps arrive even before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were members of the Green Berets from the Golaja sector. They had their training camp there. That's where they trained their own units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, once again I am concerned about your leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman said to us yesterday that there were certain Green Berets who retreated from Mahala to Golaja the day when the fighting erupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now when you say to him: Did Muslim soldiers open fire on Serbian soldiers who were scouring the mission, did Muslim soldiers outside of Mahala arrive in Mahala on that day, those are leading questions. They only undermine the probative value of the witness testimony because they come from your mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid putting leading questions to you, kindly tell us briefly what happened on that day when you scoured the terrain in Mahala, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day members -- or rather, armed Muslims were invited to surrender their weapons. A dead-line was set. I believe that it was at 12.00, but I can't be sure of that. They were invited to come out before 12.00 and to surrender their weapons or operations would be launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the operation was indeed launched?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the operation was launched. In Mahala itself there was no serious fighting. It is my own personal assumption based on what I learned that they had probably estimated that they cannot put up significant resistance and they withdrew in the direction of Golaja mountain. They had their camps there. And before that some of those civilians, i.e., women and children, had left Mahala. I forgot to say that. They left before the operation was even launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at another document. The Prosecutor tendered it, P2408. This is the title page. We are interested in the following page. The document is dated 30th May 1992. It was issued by the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most Serbian municipality. It's an order to the Serbian Territorial Defence: "Hereby the Serbian Territorial Defence is duty-bound to prevent all persons from entering the Mahala area except for authorised organs who are involved in the activity of mopping up Mahala."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, was the Crisis Staff in a position to issue orders to the Serbian Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't confirm whether they could or couldn't do that. In any case, this shows that the Crisis Staff did issue such an order to the Territorial Defence, an order to that effect, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to call up P3302.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a transcript of a radio show. It was shown to you yesterday. You were also shown the English page 7 and the B/C/S page 11 in this document. On the female voice here we can see at the bottom in the last sentence in B/C/S version, line 7 in English: "If you do want to go on living in these territories, accept co-operation, hand over all the weapons and military equipment ..." In the territory of Sanski Most, to the best of your knowledge, who was it who started the conflict, the Muslim side? The Serbian side? Who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most, as far as I know, the first conflicts were caused by the Muslim side in Hambarine, as far as I know, when a vehicle was attacked of the members of the 6th Sana Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Serb authorities, military and civilian, did they offer co-operation on other occasions like this one too, that is to say, to the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, co-operation was always offered to all in order to avoid bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now briefly let us take a look at 65 ter 3184 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, such general -- were you nice? Did you co-operate? Did you co-operate at all times? Did you co-operate at every occasion? Doesn't assist the Chamber. If you want to clearly show these kinds of things, then take an example. We have had -- only ten minutes ago I asked for one concrete example on one of the answers given on such a general statement. It turned out that the witness was talking about probabilities rather than about facts. Try to avoid this kind of general sweeping statements and try to focus on facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karac, did you ever take part in any negotiations persuading people to hand over weapons? Did you go to villages to talk to people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was involved in such a conversation. I think it was the village of Tomina. I cannot say that with certainty, but I think that we even reached agreement with people that disarmament would take place and that everything would evolve peacefully. People left and after that I really never attended such meetings with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask then one thing. You told us that you sought to co-operate. I also understand from your answer that the other party also co-operated fully. Now, what happened with that village after that? Were the Muslims living there peacefully for the rest of the war time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I took part in these talks, that the representatives of the other side accepted and we had reached agreement. However, that was not observed, and I'm going to give you quite a few examples of Muslims living --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you may elaborate on that one example but first of all please answer my question. Did they continue to live peacefully there or did they leave or did they stay, or tell us what happened with the village and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that village a military operation was carried out. Part of the people left earlier. After the operation part of them withdrew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Who carried out an operation in the village of Tomina and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Tomina we did not carry out an operation. In Tomina, Your Honour, we had a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then something happened that the villagers in Tomina apparently then finally left or partly left or -- let me see. Yes, you earlier said: "In that village," and we were talking about Tomina, "in that village a military operation was carried out." Then I asked you: "Who carried out an operation in the village of Tomina and when?" And then you say: "In Tomina we did not carry out an operation," whereas two lines before you say: "In that village a military operation was carried out." Could you explain to us whether an operation was carried out in Tomina when and by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Tomina an operation was not carried out. In Tomina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I continue? In Tomina there was only a meeting, a meeting with representatives of the surrounding villages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then what happened that made part of the population of Tomina leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that people left that area because they feared for their personal safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that is correct, that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think it is. Did you speak with anyone from Tomina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not recall the names of these people, not even the people from the Serb side because I did not live in Sanski Most. So I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the people from the Serb side leave as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were people from the Serb side who left too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they leave in the same numbers as the Muslims left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they any less concerned about the safety then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were worried about their safety too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, they did not leave in the same numbers and we know generally, including Sanski Most, that most of the Muslims left, whereas most of the Serbs stayed. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you explain to me why the Muslims were apparently in such fear that they left and did not return, whereas the Serbs mainly stayed and if they had left at least returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Muslims probably left fearing for their lives, and they wanted to go to destinations that were safer. Part of them who thought that war should be waged stayed on. The Serb population was the majority population there and they had more soldiers that had been mobilised and in a way they felt safety coming from that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the reason why they stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So finally, safety was not secured for Muslims whereas the Serbs felt that they would be safe to stay or return in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that they felt safer but not all Serbs felt safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And again, the example of Tomina shows again that we want facts, facts and not just sweeping statements. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are involved in discussions in Tomina about handing over weapons. Were the weapons handed over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Part of the weapons were handed over. It was mostly hunting weapons that were handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any weapons that had not been handed over?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, why do you think so? What weapons were not handed over and why do you think they were not handed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think -- well, our assessments were that in Golaja there were between 3- and 400 armed men and time proved that to be right. So Golaja, Your Honour, until 1993 was an unsafe area. In the evening one would not pass along that road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Golaja the village of Tomina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not, it's not, Your Honour, but people from these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Lukic, I asked about Tomina, hunting weapons were handed over. The witness asked whether there were weapons that were not handed over. He says: "I think so." And if you further explore that, it turns out that he can't tell us anything about it. He then moves to Golaja apparently which he says is not Tomina. Facts, facts, and nothing else. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These armed men at Golaja, did they come from that area, like Tomina and the surrounding villages, or had they come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Golaja, they came from Golaja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Again you are leading him. You are giving him the answer to the question. Did they come from Tomina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where did they come from, that's the non-leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Let us now take a look at 65 ter number 3184. [In English] Sorry, 31874. In this document we need page 4 in English version and page 68 in B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that part of the selection the Prosecution made?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then it's P7070.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the previous page there is that part where you marked the strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need page 68 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps I disturbed you. That was the original document if you say page 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in B/C/S it's page 68, and in translation there are only seven pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just asking if that is part of the selection made and then it would be a different e-court number of course. But if that is now the right page, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We -- now I have the right page in B/C/S and I think that translation we do have of the same page in English, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, you do recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see up here it says: "Meeting of the brigade" --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "And the battalion commander"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further down, the last asterisk, this is what it says: "There is no solution until agreement is reached between all the three peoples." Was that the position of your military unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Solution for what, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've heard the Judge's question, solution for what?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a solution for the situation that cropped up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the tensions that occurred. There was a quarrel among all three ethnic communities and solution was -- and a solution was sought to remedy that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours don't have anything else, I would move to the last document I have for this witness and finish with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we could have P2876, please. [Interpretation] So this is a document of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. The date is the 30th of May, 1992. Now that we've seen the first page, we need the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 30746 of yesterday's transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second. That's not the document I have under this number, 2867, P2867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if you say what kind of document you're seeking perhaps it could assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a meeting -- the document right in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now discuss this briefly. This is a meeting with the presidents of municipalities in the zone of responsibility of the division. It's held on the 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 30747, my learned friend Ms. Edgerton suggested the following to you and I'm going to read the question, line 11 onwards: [In English] "So when you said in your written evidence that the role of your brigade was to keep the peace between the opposing sides, that's actually incorrect, isn't it?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Bear with me. Pay attention to what is being said and what is being said is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need -- we need the previous page in English, I apologise. The very bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here: "At the end of the meeting, Colonel Galic proposed the following conclusions ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then we need the next page in English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 2 it says in the document which the Prosecutor used to corroborate that argument: "Hold the present positions and defend them without war ..." What kind of instructions did you receive? What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that war should be avoided at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, i.e., in mid-May, did the brigade command participate or did they at least try to participate in calming the situation down in the territory of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Commander Basara tried to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no day that went by when Colonel Basara didn't go to the villages with a majority Muslim population. He himself hailed from Sanski Most, he knew all those people. He went to those villages to calm the situation down in order to avert any unwanted consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karac, this is all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I'll give you an opportunity if you have any further questions. I have one question. Witness, were you aware in any way, because you told us a lot about what happened in Sanski Most, were you aware what happened with some 20 men on the 31st of May or the 1st of June which were taken from the Vrhpolje or Hrustovo area, were then escorted and were forced to jump from a bridge where then they were shot at once they were in the water? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is true, this indeed did happen. I don't know who the perpetrators of that were. I know that Colonel Basara went up there to calm the situation down. As far as I know he told me that those were people whom he didn't know and that they scattered when they had seen him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will have, Your Honour. I estimate right now about -- I'll try and aim for 10 minutes but probably 15 minutes' worth of questions after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll take a break. You may already follow the usher. We'll deal with a few administrative matters. We would like to see you back in a little bit over 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to put on the record that the 65 ter number of P7070 which was admitted at the beginning of our session today is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was and that's one of the -- it's an administrative matter that Ms. Stewart brought to my attention. I inverted the last two digits of the 65 ter number on the record at page 2 I referred to 31847 and 31847A. It should of course read 31874 and 31874A. And my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as you see, nothing escapes the attention of my colleagues. I'd briefly like to deal with the following matter, it's about scheduling and it is about the last week of May of this year. That week starts with the 25th, which is a Monday, of May which is a holiday. Therefore, four days would remain. The Chamber is unable to sit on the 28th, that is Thursday, and the 29th, the Friday, for certain, which would leave in that week two days, that is, the 26th and the 27th of May. The -- it came to the mind of the Chamber that the parties - and I'm also looking at Defence - might prefer to sit in the week before that, that is, the week starting Monday, the 18th of May, to sit the full five days and then to sit the week after, that is, the week starting with Monday, the 1st of June, also to sit five full days, which would compensate for not sitting at all in the week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, I warned you yesterday. This is the last warning. If there is any other communication with the public gallery, you'll be removed from the courtroom. So rather turn your back to the public gallery so as -- in order to avoid any further incidents. No, I'm not asking for any comment. You can tell counsel what you want to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll probably have to consult with Mr. Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and I'm very pro this proposal but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would then have two weeks of five days but one full week break between the two. We'd like to hear from you if possible after the break. And of course from the Prosecution as well, but you don't have to consult a client. Then I would -- we'll now take the break. We resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, it may have been a busy break, Mr. Lukic. Any results from your consultations as far as the last week of May is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, your offer is accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, it wasn't an offer. But then Prosecution, any problems in having a non-sitting week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, of course that would be fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's hereby decided that we'll sit in the week of the 18th of May, we sit the full five days. We'll sit in the week of the 1st of June, the full five days. And we'll not sit in the week starting the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Karac, with regard to your testimony today, my colleague showed you P2411, at temporary transcript page 3. And just so you can be sure of your answers, maybe we should just call these documents up as I go through them, please, P2411. So this is an order from the TO commander Anicic for operations against a number of locations in co-ordination with 6th Brigade units. And my colleague Mr. Lukic asked you and you told him that you knew who Colonel Anicic was, and that was at temporary transcript page 4. And then he showed you P2408 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could see that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- at temporary transcript page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And go over to page 2 in B/C/S and in English, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is a document, the document you saw from the Crisis Staff for Sanski Most Serbian municipality to the Serbian Territorial Defence, dated 30 May 1992, to prevent all persons from entering Mahala --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the right B/C/S page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, we don't. Pardon me, I hadn't realised that there was an authentication page. So if we could go to the next page, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Often it's the back of the page -- previous page. No. We're now moving in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar I think was having -- there was some functionality problems with e-court when he came on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Otherwise we should print out the B/C/S version and give it to the witness or read it literally to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. So that's the other document he showed you, P2408, to prevent all persons from entering Mahala except for those for authorised organs who were involved in the activity of mopping up. And he asked you based on this whether the Crisis Staff was in a position to issue orders to the Territorial Defence, and you said that you couldn't confirm but in any case this document shows that they did. Now, my question to you is this: Since you know who Anicic was, you would know, wouldn't you, that on the very same day, 30 May 1992, that this order was issued, Nedjo Anicic, the TO commander, was on, he was a member of, the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic also took you back to your notebook that we had talked about yesterday, P7070, and you looked at or we looked at B/C/S page 3 and English translation page 4. And he took you down to the asterisked points and in particular the last one where it said: "There is no solution until agreement is reached between all three peoples." Then he asked you: "Was that the position of your military unit?" And you said: "Yes." And His Honour Judge Orie said: "Solution for what?" Now, your response was: "This is a solution for the situation that cropped up in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the tensions that occurred. There was a quarrel among all three ethnic communities and the solution was -- and a solution was sought to remedy that." Now, that solution involved ethnic relocation, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document before me. May I be allowed to see it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As soon as we've got some functionality restored to e-court, I think that won't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P7070, B/C/S page 7, English page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have that one in B/C/S as well if it can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we at least would need the English on the screen as well in order for us to be able to follow. P7070, any way to get it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just have a copy of the English printed up immediately. The one I have in my hand is marked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, there we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the right page, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the English back. And in B/C/S it's the right side of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So can you answer my question now? That solution involved ethnic relocation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KARAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were talks of one of such options. There were options. There were talks of options, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no further questions for you, Witness. Therefore, I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher. And the usher is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- invited to bring the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you wanted to raise the matter with one of the D documents which we were informed you would like to raise, that was D --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to inform Your Honours that we sent it for translation and we expect to have it translated on Friday, this Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your next witness would be Mr. Predojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and he will be led by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. Perhaps I briefly deal with one matter, it's about the statement of Slavko Mijanovic. During the testimony of this witness on the 25th of November of last year, the Chamber marked document D799, which is Mijanovic's Rule 92 ter statement, for identification pending a new English translation. This is to be found at transcript pages 28799 to 801. The Defence informed the Chamber via e-mail on the 19th of January that the requested revised English translation of D799 had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D18-3069. The Prosecution does not object to the translation or the admission of D799 as far as we are aware of and what we see on the transcript and which was also confirmed in an e-mail from the Prosecution of the 19th of January. The Chamber hereby instructs the court officer to replace the existing English translation with the revised translation and admits D799 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. It's not very polite of us to continue with other matters when you entered the courtroom, Mr. Predojevic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. Could I invite you to stand and to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Predojevic. You'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our usual form, I would like to ask you to speak slowly and give us your exact first and last names.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Predojevic, at one point in time did you give a statement in writing to General Mladic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have 65 ter 1D01709 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Predojevic, you have a screen in front of you and you can see a text on that screen. So if you do see this in front of you, this is what I'm going to ask you: Do you see a signature on that text; and if so, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: I see the signature and it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please look at the last page of this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The question is the same, Mr. Predojevic. On this page is the signature yours again? And the date that can be seen here, was it entered in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature and the date is written in my own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Predojevic, when preparing to appear in this courtroom, did you tell me that it was necessary for me to ask you something about a few things in your statement in order to spell some things out more precisely and to clarify certain matters?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please take a look at paragraph 5 of your statement. Now I would just like to ask you to take a look at this and please follow what I'll be saying. I would like to indicate what it was that you had indicated; namely, that in the first sentence before the words "until the end of the war," or "throughout the war," it should say: "Until the 12th of September, 1994, when I was wounded. And after returning from sick leave from March 1995 until the 11th of October, 1995, I carried out the duties of assistant commander for intelligence affairs in the brigade command and afterwards deputy commander of the assault detachment in the Sana Brigade," and it is only then that the words "to the end of the war" are inserted again. Is this what you found necessary to insert?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 6, in the second sentence, did you indicate to me that in order to be as precise as possible instead of the words "the VRS forces" or, rather, "the 6th Sana Brigade," it should say "the forces of the JNA, the JNA forces"? Then in the same sentence, for the sake of precision, after the words "in the liberation," the words "of the building of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most" should be inserted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 13, so let us please look at paragraph 13 of your statement. Did you indicate to me that for the sake of precision in your statement you said that you wanted to add in the first sentence after the words "of about 30 men," you would like to add the date, the 7th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to end with paragraph 15. Please focus on this. Did you tell me that in the second sentence, after the word "replenish" we should add the prefix "and," meaning to say: We replenished our units with members of the disbanded paramilitary forces as well. And then there are the words "personnel, military personnel," and you wanted to add the words "my battalion, of my battalion." And finally in the same sentence, at the end certain toponyms should be added. After Usorci, the toponyms Stari Majdan, Dzevar, and Sanski Most should be added?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've made these amendments and clarifications, today in this courtroom when you took the solemn declaration stating that you would tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, would you give identical answers if the same questions were to be put to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These questions, would they be based on the best of your recollection and knowledge in terms of what it is that you are testifying about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Answers.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: The answers would be as you have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the statement along with these amendments, the statement of Branko Predojevic. At this moment it is marked 65 ter 1D01709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No objections to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the statement receives number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D881, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to tender two associated exhibits, 65 ter 1D02977 and 1D02978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D02977 receives Exhibit Number D882. Document number 1D02978 receives Exhibit D883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D882 and D883 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, I would like to read out a summary of the statement of Witness Branko Predojevic. Thank you. Witness Branko Predojevic as a reserve officer of the JNA and a teacher of defence towards the end of 1991 became professionally involved in the then-JNA and after its withdrawal from Croatia he came, together with his unit, to Bileca and from there to Nevesinje in BiH. After the withdrawal of the JNA from BiH in May 1992, since he was born in BH he joined the VRS and was assigned to the Nevesinje Brigade. On the 22nd of June, 1992, he took over the duty of battalion commander in the 6th Sana Brigade in Sanski Most. And he remained in that position all the way up until he was wounded on the 12th of September, 1994. He speaks about the attitude of the VRS towards paramilitary formations, especially SOS, the Serb Defence Forces, in Sanski Most. He says that part of this unit was attached to his unit. He claims that the VRS was never involved in moving out the civilian population from Sanski Most and they carried out only military tasks. The VRS functioned completely separate from the Crisis Staff, asking that they do not interfere in each other's affairs in the domain of the military. He knows that the officers of the VRS did attend meetings of the Crisis Staff but they did not have the right to vote and could not take decisions at Crisis Staff meetings. During his service he did not receive a single order that was in contravention of any law or customs of war or against the civilian population or civilian property and facilities. In the period of 1992 and 1993, it did happen that they had prisoners of war and there was a direct command that these persons should be treated only on the basis of regulations and customs of war. Finally, he speaks of two documents that corroborate his statement. One has to do with the criminal report against members of his brigade who they realised had committed murder of several civilians. The other document is a document of the commander regarding the treatment of paramilitary and volunteer units. That would be the summary, Your Honours, and I would just like to put a few additional questions to him in order to clarify certain matters that are contained in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at paragraph 19 of D881 which is Mr. Predojevic's statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before you ask questions, I want some clarification from the summary here. You say in the summary, Mr. Stojanovic, at page 38, lines -- line -- starting from line 2, you say: "He speaks about the attitude of the VRS towards paramilitary formations, especially SOS, the Serb Defence Forces, in Sanski Most. He says that part of this unit was attached to his unit." Is it part of the SOS or part of the -- part of his unit was the SOS or was it the paramilitary? Or in fact the paramilitary -- is the SOS a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me, then according to the witness's statement, according to the witness's statement, paragraph 13 of his statement, the answer would be yes, he treats them as a paramilitary unit and he adds that they were attached to his unit on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Predojevic, look at paragraph 19. We have to be as precise as possible here. We need to provide as many concrete examples and facts as possible. Therefore, could you please tell the Trial Chamber about POWs, those you captured during operations. What POWs did you have in mind, in what part of the battle-field, when you mentioned the years 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: I meant the POWs from the Muslim army. That happened at the Gradacac front line. There were subsequent captures but not by my battalion, but rather, various units of the brigade. For example, in 1995 near Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For precision's sake, could you tell the Trial Chamber and all of us in the courtroom, where is Gradacac? Where was the Gradacac battle-field? In geographic terms, how far was that from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: That battle-field or that town was some 200 kilometres from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to ask you this: Throughout your membership in the Army of Republika Srpska, bearing in mind the war path of your battalion, could you please tell the Trial Chamber where were you and your unit or at least a part thereof deployed during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, the first deployment of my unit was in the Bihac theatre of war in mid-July 1992. We were there for no more than three or four days all together. After that, in mid-July I took my unit to the corridor to the territory of Odzak. It was the Tactical Group 1 which was engaged in the breakthrough of the corridor. After that, I took my unit to the Modrica sector or the Ploce sector, or rather, the Pelagicevo sector. That was sometime in August 1992. After that, we were deployed to the theatre near Brod where we participated in combat operations to liberate Brod. We were there up until the moment Brod was liberated. Then we went back to the Gradacac battle-field. That's where my unit was most commonly deployed. At the beginning of 1993, or rather, in early February 1993, until the 7th of March, we were in Bratunac. After a short rest, we were sent to the Bihac theatre at the beginning of April, on the 7th of April that was. We stayed there for a month or so. After that, for a rather long period of time we stayed in Gracac or in Pelagicevo to be more precise. That's where we were stationed until the beginning of 1994 -- sorry, not beginning of 1994, until September 1994. In September 1994 we went to Suva Medja in Novi Grad municipality. I stayed there until the 12th of September together with my unit. That's when I was wounded. After that I was on sick leave for nearly six months. And then at the end of February 1995, upon return to the unit, I was assigned the position of assistant commander for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up D882. This is the number that the document bears at the moment, D882.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of your statement, Mr. Predojevic, you speak about the criminal report that was filed against a member of your brigade. You see that in front of you at the moment. The date is 5 December 1992. Please tell the Court, during that period of time, i.e., the beginning of December 1992, where were you physically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time I and my unit were in the theatre of war near Gradacac, and that member of my unit went home for the burial of his relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this crime, did it happen while that member of unit was in Sanski Most where he attended the burial of his relative?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: When we returned home I learned about that incident. He was on furlough at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please help us. Which member are you referring to? This criminal report refers to five different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the witness, Your Honour. In any case, it would have been my question anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Predojevic, you have that criminal report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it is against five different people, Gvozden, Mile - I don't know if the family name is spelled correctly - Miroslav Gvozden, Bojan Gvozden, Ostoja Gvozden, and the minor Zoran Simcic. Could you please tell the Court which of them were members of your unit, more specifically of that unit of yours?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mile Gvozden was. I suppose that the others were members of my unit as well, but I remember Mile Gvozden. My unit was replenished from that village. Mile Gvozden, I'm sure. And the others if they were militarily able-bodied men, they were members of my unit. But there were over a thousand members in that unit over time so I can't remember everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you say Gvozden, Mile, who do you have in mind just for the record, could you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Milan Gvozden is who I have in mind, to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Under what number is he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And may I clarify the matter further. Was this the person you said -- you were asked: "And this crime, did it happen while that member of unit was in Sanski Most where he attended the burial of his relative?" Is that the person under number 1 or another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the person number 1, that person was on furlough at the time. He had been asked to accompany the dead body and help the family to organise the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That clarifies the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now let's look at D881, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just briefly ask, I'll not further elaborate on it, but do you know what happened with this criminal report, whether any follow-up was given? Were they prosecuted? Were they punished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you, at least not in very precise terms because that member of the unit and the perpetrator of that crime after a certain while returned to my unit. It was common practice after the war to prosecute all such persons who had committed similar offences, and legal measures were taken against them as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did the perpetrator return to your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you when exactly, but I know that he returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it after a week? After a month? After a year? After three years? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately after two or three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever inquire why he was not prosecuted at that time? Because you had a likely murderer now within your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already told you, it was common practice. Instead of putting somebody in jail, and thus exempting him from war duty, they were recruited into units where they spent some time. And then when the time came, they were prosecuted. I know that many of them who had committed such and similar crimes after the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you didn't know during the war that they would be prosecuted after the war, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had to know. Nobody could go unpunished. It was not an isolated case. There were several such people. For example, I myself can give you at least the names of two other criminals of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I accept that some people were prosecuted after the war, but during the war how could you possibly know that they would be prosecuted after the war? Was it announced somewhere? Was it -- were you -- was there an order to say: Well, he should return to his unit but we'll prosecute him once the war is over? Is there any evidence that would support your suggestion that one could know during the war that murderers would just return to the unit and then in the expectation that they would later be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received that information from our superior command, and I'm conveying it to you. According to that information, when peace came he would be prosecuted. And it was thought at the time that a bigger punishment for him was to be in the unit than to be put in jail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour. My colleague Mr. Lukic has just indicated to me that one part of his answer to your last question has not been recorded. Can I repeat the question? I don't want to lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can take him to the portion which was translated and then ask him what he said after that. Otherwise, we would have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the position was that it was better for him to be in jail than in the unit, and what followed that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that the position was - hence the solution - that it was better both for -- it was better for the unit for him to be a member of the unit. That for him to be in jail would have given him more protection than being in the unit. And then when conditions were ripe, a full criminal procedure would be taken. And that was really done. In addition to him, I can remember two other people that fared the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the sake of clarification, please look at paragraph 16 which is in front of you, Mr. Predojevic. When you say that the VRS was never involved in any removal of civilian population from Sanski Most, are you referring to 20 June 1992, the date when you arrived in Sanski Most, or are you referring to the time before that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only testify about the time when I joined the Sana Brigade onwards. And as to what happened earlier, this can only be hearsay because I can only share with you the stories that I heard from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Predojevic, for all your answers. At the moment we don't have any other questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Jeremy, would you prefer to take the break now and then have the cross-examination in one flow or rather start now for the next five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd prefer to take the break now, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Predojevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You'll find Mr. Jeremy to your right. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you've already provided in some detail the various war theatres that you were in outside of Sanski Most during the war period and I'd just like to seek a little bit more clarity on your whereabouts during that period. Now, you mentioned that you were wounded in September 1994 and you returned back to duty in March 1995. Where were you when you were recovering from your injuries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
utterances.text: I recovered first of all at the Prijedor hospital, and after that in the house in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir, I'll repeat my question. How long were you in Prijedor after you were injured? If you went there in September 1994, when did you return back to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO PREDOJEVIC
